claim: The dendritic arbors of hippocampal pyramidal neurons in Cd40-/- mice were dramatically stunted compared with those of Cd40+/+ littermates at postnatal day 10.
source: Golgi preparations carried out on Cd40+/+ and Cd40-/- mice at postnatal day 10 (P10) revealed that the size and complexity of the dendritic arbors of hippocampal pyramidal neurons and striatal MSNs were markedly affected in the absence of CD40, but in opposite ways. The dendritic arbors of the excitatory pyramidal neurons of the CA fields of the hippocampus of Cd40-/- mice were dramatically stunted compared with those of Cd40+/+ littermates (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Golgi preparation data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text, comparing Cd40+/+ and Cd40-/- mice at P10.

claim: The reduction of dendrite size and complexity in Cd40-/- mice affected both apical and basal dendrite compartments of hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: Representative high power images show that the reduction of dendrite size and complexity in Cd40-/- mice affected both apical and basal dendrite compartments of these excitatory neurons (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-power microscopy images in Figure 1B showing both apical and basal dendrite compartments.

claim: Total dendrite length in the apical compartment of CA1 pyramidal neurons was significantly reduced in Cd40-/- mice compared with Cd40+/+ littermates (p=6.02×10−16).
source: This revealed marked and highly significant reductions in total dendrite length in both apical (p=6.02×10−16) and basal (p=4.75×10−14) compartments of Cd40-/- mice compared with Cd40+/+ littermates (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length shown in Figure 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: Total dendrite length in the basal compartment of CA1 pyramidal neurons was significantly reduced in Cd40-/- mice compared with Cd40+/+ littermates (p=4.75×10−14).
source: This revealed marked and highly significant reductions in total dendrite length in both apical (p=6.02×10−16) and basal (p=4.75×10−14) compartments of Cd40-/- mice compared with Cd40+/+ littermates (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length shown in Figure 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: Sholl analysis showed significant differences in branching patterns between Cd40+/+ and Cd40-/- mice for both apical dendrites (p=1.67×10−14) and basal dendrites (p=4.75×10−5) of CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: These reductions were in reflected in the Sholl analyses (Figure 1D), which plot branching in the dendrite arbors with distance from the cell body (two-way ANOVA Cd40+/+ versus Cd40-/-, p=1.67×10−14, apical dendrites and p=4.75×10−5, basal dendrites).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis using two-way ANOVA.

claim: The number of branch points in the apical dendrite compartment of CA1 pyramidal neurons was significantly reduced in Cd40-/- mice (p=8.85×10−7).
source: Accordingly, quantification of the number of branch points in these dendrite compartments showed clear statistically significant reductions in Cd40-/- mice (p=8.85×10−7, apical and p=6.48×10−8, basal), however there was no significant difference (p=0.82) in the number of primary dendrites between the pyramidal neurons of Cd40-/- and Cd40+/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of branch points shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: The number of branch points in the basal dendrite compartment of CA1 pyramidal neurons was significantly reduced in Cd40-/- mice (p=6.48×10−8).
source: Accordingly, quantification of the number of branch points in these dendrite compartments showed clear statistically significant reductions in Cd40-/- mice (p=8.85×10−7, apical and p=6.48×10−8, basal), however there was no significant difference (p=0.82) in the number of primary dendrites between the pyramidal neurons of Cd40-/- and Cd40+/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of branch points shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of primary dendrites between CA1 pyramidal neurons of Cd40-/- and Cd40+/+ mice (p=0.82).
source: Accordingly, quantification of the number of branch points in these dendrite compartments showed clear statistically significant reductions in Cd40-/- mice (p=8.85×10−7, apical and p=6.48×10−8, basal), however there was no significant difference (p=0.82) in the number of primary dendrites between the pyramidal neurons of Cd40-/- and Cd40+/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of primary dendrites shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: CD40 plays a major role in promoting the growth and elaboration of hippocampal pyramidal neuron dendrites.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that CD40 plays a major role in promoting the growth and elaboration of hippocampal pyramidal neuron dendrites.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data showing reduced dendrite growth in Cd40-/- mice.

claim: The dendritic arbors of striatal MSNs in Cd40-/- mice were very much larger and more profuse than those of Cd40+/+ littermates.
source: In marked contrast to hippocampal excitatory neurons, the dendritic arbors of the striatal MSNs of Cd40-/- mice were very much larger and more profuse than those of Cd40+/+ littermates (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Golgi preparation images shown in Figure 1E and F comparing Cd40+/+ and Cd40-/- mice.

claim: Total dendrite length of striatal MSNs was significantly increased in Cd40-/- mice compared with Cd40+/+ littermates (p=6.87×10−17).
source: Quantification of total dendrite length revealed a marked and highly significant increase in Cd40-/- mice compared with Cd40+/+ littermates (p=6.87×10−17) (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length shown in Figure 1G with statistical analysis.

claim: Sholl analysis of MSN dendrites showed significant differences between Cd40+/+ and Cd40-/- mice (p=6.68×10−4).
source: This increase in dendrite size was in reflected in the Sholl analysis (Figure 1H) (two-way ANOVA Cd40+/+ versus Cd40-/-, p=6.68×10−4).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 1H with statistical analysis using two-way ANOVA.

claim: The number of branch points in MSN dendrites showed a 49% increase in Cd40-/- mice (p=1.13×10−13).
source: Quantification of the number of branch points in these dendrite compartments showed clear statistically significant increase in Cd40-/- mice (49% increase, p=1.13×10−13), and as with hippocampal pyramidal neurons, there was no significant difference in the number of primary dendrites in the MSNs of Cd40-/- and Cd40+/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of branch points shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of primary dendrites in MSNs between Cd40-/- and Cd40+/+ mice.
source: Quantification of the number of branch points in these dendrite compartments showed clear statistically significant increase in Cd40-/- mice (49% increase, p=1.13×10−13), and as with hippocampal pyramidal neurons, there was no significant difference in the number of primary dendrites in the MSNs of Cd40-/- and Cd40+/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of primary dendrites shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: CD40 plays a major role in restricting the growth and elaboration of MSN dendrites in the developing striatum.
source: These findings indicate that CD40 plays a major role in restricting the growth and elaboration of MSN dendrites in the developing striatum.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data showing increased dendrite growth in Cd40-/- MSNs.

claim: Hippocampal pyramidal neuron dendrite arbors were clearly stunted in Cd40-/- mice compared with Cd40+/+ littermates at P30 and in adults.
source: Golgi preparations revealed that hippocampal pyramidal neuron dendrite arbors were clearly stunted in Cd40-/- mice compared with Cd40+/+ littermates whereas striatal MSN dendrite arbors of Cd40-/- mice were much larger and more complex than those of Cd40+/+ littermates both ages (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Golgi preparation images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 comparing P30 and adult mice.

claim: Striatal MSN dendrite arbors of Cd40-/- mice were much larger and more complex than those of Cd40+/+ littermates at P30 and in adults.
source: Golgi preparations revealed that hippocampal pyramidal neuron dendrite arbors were clearly stunted in Cd40-/- mice compared with Cd40+/+ littermates whereas striatal MSN dendrite arbors of Cd40-/- mice were much larger and more complex than those of Cd40+/+ littermates both ages (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Golgi preparation images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 comparing P30 and adult mice.

claim: The distinctive phenotypic changes evident in the dendrite arbors of both hippocampal pyramidal neurons and striatal MSNs observed in the early postnatal period are maintained throughout life.
source: This shows that the distinctive phenotypic changes evident in the dendrite arbors of both kinds neurons observed in the early postnatal period are maintained throughout life.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data from P10, P30, and adult mice showing persistent phenotypic differences.

claim: Hippocampal pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40-/- mice were smaller than those cultured from Cd40+/+ mice.
source: Similar to the phenotypic changes observed in Golgi preparations of Cd40-/- mice, pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40-/- mice were smaller than those cultured from Cd40+/+ mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by images of cultured neurons shown in Figure 2A comparing Cd40+/+ and Cd40-/- mice.

claim: Total dendrite length in cultured hippocampal pyramidal neurons was significantly reduced in cultures from Cd40-/- mice compared with Cd40+/+ mice (p=2.9×10−6).
source: Measurement of the total dendrite length in the dendrite arbors of individual neurons revealed a highly significant reduction in cultures established from Cd40-/- mice compared with those cultured from Cd40+/+ mice (p=2.9×10−6) (Figure 2B), but no significant difference in the number of primary dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length in cultured neurons shown in Figure 2B with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of primary dendrites between cultured hippocampal pyramidal neurons from Cd40-/- and Cd40+/+ mice.
source: Measurement of the total dendrite length in the dendrite arbors of individual neurons revealed a highly significant reduction in cultures established from Cd40-/- mice compared with those cultured from Cd40+/+ mice (p=2.9×10−6) (Figure 2B), but no significant difference in the number of primary dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of primary dendrites shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The morphologies of hippocampal pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40+/+ and Cd40-/- mice reflect the phenotypic differences observed in vivo.
source: These data suggest that the morphologies of hippocampal pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40+/+ and Cd40-/- mice reflect the phenotypic differences observed in vivo.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation comparing in vitro culture data with in vivo Golgi preparation data.

claim: Treatment of pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40+/+ mice with soluble CD40L significantly reduced dendrite length to the same extent as that observed in untreated pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40-/- mice (p=1.1×10−8).
source: Treatment of pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40+/+ mice with soluble CD40L significantly reduced dendrite length to the same extent as that observed in untreated pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40-/- mice (p=1.1×10−8) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length in cultured neurons treated with soluble CD40L shown in Figure 2B with statistical analysis.

claim: Neither soluble CD40 (CD40-Fc chimera) nor control Fc protein had any significant effect on dendrite growth from pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40+/+ mice.
source: Neither soluble CD40 (CD40-Fc chimera, in which the extracellular domain of CD40 is linked to the Fc part of human IgG1) nor control Fc protein had any significant effect on dendrite growth from pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40+/+ mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length in cultured neurons treated with CD40-Fc or Fc protein shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CD40L did not significantly affect dendrite growth from pyramidal neurons of Cd40-/- mice.
source: While CD40L reduced dendrite growth from wild type neurons, it did not significantly affect dendrite growth from pyramidal neurons of Cd40-/- mice (Figure 2B), suggesting that CD40L does not exert a non-specific suppressive effect on dendrite growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length in cultured Cd40-/- neurons treated with CD40L shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Addition of CD40L to pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40+/+ mice competes with endogenous membrane integrated CD40L for binding to endogenous CD40, thereby blocking CD40-activated CD40L-mediated reverse signalling.
source: The most parsimonious explanation for these results is that addition of CD40L to pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40+/+ mice competes with endogenous membrane integrated CD40L for binding to endogenous CD40, thereby blocking CD40-activated CD40L-mediated reverse signalling.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental results showing that soluble CD40L reduces dendrite growth in wild-type neurons.

claim: CD40-Fc, but not Fc control protein, fully restored the reduced dendrite growth phenotype of pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40-/- mice (p=6.5×10−3).
source: CD40-Fc, but not Fc control protein, fully restored the reduced dendrite growth phenotype of pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40-/- mice (p=6.5×10−3) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length in cultured Cd40-/- neurons treated with CD40-Fc shown in Figure 2B with statistical analysis.

claim: CD40-activated CD40L mediated reverse signalling promotes dendrite growth from developing hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that CD40-activated CD40L mediated reverse signalling promotes dendrite growth from developing hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental results from CD40L and CD40-Fc treatments in cultured neurons.

claim: The axons of pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40-/- mice were significantly shorter than the axons of neurons cultured from Cd40+/+ mice in both 3 day and 9 day cultures (p=7.8×10−12, 3 days; p=1.3×10−4, 9 days).
source: The axons of pyramidal neurons cultured from Cd40-/- mice were significantly shorter than the axons of neurons cultured from Cd40+/+ mice in both 3 day and 9 day cultures (p=7.8×10−12, 3 days; p=1.3×10−4, 9 days).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of axon length in cultured neurons shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis.

claim: CD40L, but not CD40-Fc, suppressed axon growth from Cd40+/+ neurons to the same extend as that observed in untreated Cd40-/- neurons (p=6.4×10−11, 3 days; p=1.2×10−5, 9 days).
source: CD40L, but not CD40-Fc, suppressed axon growth from Cd40+/+ neurons to the same extend as that observed in untreated Cd40-/- neurons (p=6.4×10−11, 3 days; p=1.2×10−5, 9 days).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of axon length in cultured neurons treated with CD40L or CD40-Fc shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis.

claim: The reduced axon growth phenotype of neurons of Cd40-/- mice was completely rescued by CD40-Fc (p=2.6×10−5, 3 days; p=4.9×10−6, 9 days).
source: The reduced axon growth phenotype of neurons of Cd40-/- mice was completely rescued by CD40-Fc (p=2.6×10−5, 3 days; p=4.9×10−6, 9 days).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of axon length in cultured Cd40-/- neurons treated with CD40-Fc shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis.

claim: CD40-activated CD40L-mediated reverse signalling enhances axon growth from developing hippocampal pyramidal neurons in culture.
source: These results suggest that CD40-activated CD40L-mediated reverse signalling also enhances axon growth from developing hippocampal pyramidal neurons in culture.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental results showing effects of CD40L and CD40-Fc on axon growth in cultured neurons.

claim: The full extent of hippocampal pyramidal axons cannot be reliably discerned in Golgi preparations.
source: However, because the full extent of these axons cannot be reliably discerned in Golgi preparations, we cannot definitively conclude that CD40L reverse signalling enhances the growth of pyramidal axons in vivo.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the limitations of the Golgi preparation method for visualizing axons.

claim: The neurite arbors of MSNs cultured from Cd40-/- mice were larger than those of MSNs cultured from Cd40+/+ mice.
source: Similar to the phenotypic changes observed in Golgi preparations of Cd40-/- mice, the neurite arbors of MSNs cultured from Cd40-/- mice were larger than those of MSNs cultured from Cd40+/+ mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by images of cultured MSNs shown in Figure 4A comparing Cd40+/+ and Cd40-/- mice.

claim: Total neurite length of cultured MSNs was significantly increased in neurons from Cd40-/- mice compared with those from Cd40+/+ littermates (p=7.2×10−10).
source: Although dendrites and axons cannot be easily distinguished in these cultures, measurement of total neurite length confirmed highly significant increases in neurons cultured from Cd40-/- mice compared with those cultured from Cd40+/+ littermates (p=7.2×10−10) (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of neurite length in cultured MSNs shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis.

claim: The morphologies of MSNs cultured from Cd40+/+ and Cd40-/- mice reflect the phenotypic differences observed in vivo.
source: This suggests, as with hippocampal pyramidal neurons, that the morphologies of MSNs cultured from Cd40+/+ and Cd40-/- mice reflect the phenotypic differences observed in vivo.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation comparing in vitro culture data with in vivo Golgi preparation data for MSNs.

claim: Treatment of MSNs cultured from Cd40+/+ mice with soluble CD40L caused a significant increase in total neurite length (p=1.57×10−6) that was similar to the total neurite length observed in untreated MSNs cultured from Cd40-/- mice.
source: Treatment of MSNs cultured from Cd40+/+ mice with soluble CD40L caused a significant increase in total neurite length (p=1.57×10−6) that was similar to the total neurite length observed in untreated MSNs cultured from Cd40-/- mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of neurite length in cultured MSNs treated with soluble CD40L shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis.

claim: CD40-Fc did not affect neurite growth from MSNs cultured from Cd40+/+ mice.
source: CD40-Fc did not affect neurite growth from MSNs cultured from Cd40+/+ mice, but significantly reduced the more exuberant neurite growth of MSNs cultured from Cd40-/- mice (p=3.6×10−14) to the level observed in untreated MSNs cultured from Cd40+/+ mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of neurite length in cultured MSNs treated with CD40-Fc shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CD40-Fc significantly reduced the more exuberant neurite growth of MSNs cultured from Cd40-/- mice (p=3.6×10−14) to the level observed in untreated MSNs cultured from Cd40+/+ mice.
source: CD40-Fc did not affect neurite growth from MSNs cultured from Cd40+/+ mice, but significantly reduced the more exuberant neurite growth of MSNs cultured from Cd40-/- mice (p=3.6×10−14) to the level observed in untreated MSNs cultured from Cd40+/+ mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of neurite length in cultured Cd40-/- MSNs treated with CD40-Fc shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis.

claim: CD40 normally restricts the growth of neural processes from developing MSNs by a CD40L-mediated reverse signalling mechanism.
source: These observations suggest that CD40 normally restricts the growth of neural processes from developing MSNs by a CD40L-mediated reverse signalling mechanism.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental results from CD40L and CD40-Fc treatments in cultured MSNs.

claim: Activation of protein kinase C (PKC) is an essential step in the axon growth response of developing sympathetic neurons to TNFR1-activated TNFα-mediated reverse signaling.
source: Because we have shown that activation of protein kinase C (PKC) is an essential step in the axon growth response of developing sympathetic neurons to TNFR1-activated TNFα-mediated reverse signaling (Kisiswa et al., 2017), we investigated whether PKC plays a role in mediating the divergent effects CD40-activated CD40L reverse signalling on dendrite growth in excitatory and/or inhibitory neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Kisiswa et al., 2017).

claim: The significant restoration of dendrite growth by CD40-Fc in cultures of hippocampal pyramidal neurons from Cd40-/- mice (p=3.8×10−4) was completely prevented by Go6983 (p=1.6×10−5).
source: In cultures of hippocampal pyramidal neurons established from E18 Cd40-/- mice, the significant restoration of dendrite growth by CD40-Fc (p=3.8×10−4, Fc treatment compared with CD40-Fc treatment) was completely prevented by Go6983 (p=1.6×10−5, CD40-Fc treatment compared with CD40-Fc plus Go6983 treatment), although Go6983 had no effect on dendrite growth on its own (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length in cultured neurons treated with CD40-Fc and Go6983 shown in Figure 5A and B with statistical analysis.

claim: Go6983 had no effect on dendrite growth from hippocampal pyramidal neurons on its own.
source: In cultures of hippocampal pyramidal neurons established from E18 Cd40-/- mice, the significant restoration of dendrite growth by CD40-Fc (p=3.8×10−4, Fc treatment compared with CD40-Fc treatment) was completely prevented by Go6983 (p=1.6×10−5, CD40-Fc treatment compared with CD40-Fc plus Go6983 treatment), although Go6983 had no effect on dendrite growth on its own (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length in cultured neurons treated with Go6983 alone shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: PMA significantly rescued the stunted dendrite phenotype of hippocampal pyramidal neurons established from Cd40-/- mice (p=1.6×10−2) almost as effectively as CD40-Fc.
source: PMA significantly rescued the stunted dendrite phenotype of hippocampal pyramidal neurons established from Cd40-/- mice (p=1.6×10−2) almost as effectively as CD40-Fc (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length in cultured Cd40-/- neurons treated with PMA shown in Figure 5A and B with statistical analysis.

claim: DMSO, the vehicle for Go6983 and PMA, had no significant effect on dendrite growth from hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: DMSO, the vehicle for Go6983 and PMA, had no significant effect on dendrite growth (not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text as a control experiment result.

claim: Neither Go6983 nor PMA had any significant effect on the number of pyramidal neuron primary dendrites.
source: Neither Go6983 nor PMA had any significant effect on the number of pyramidal neuron primary dendrites (not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text as an experimental result.

claim: PKC activation mediates the effect of CD40-activated CD40L-mediated reverse signalling on dendrite growth from developing hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: These results suggest that PKC activation mediates the effect of CD40-activated CD40L-mediated reverse signalling on dendrite growth from developing hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental results showing effects of PKC inhibition and activation on dendrite growth in hippocampal neurons.

claim: The significant suppression of dendrite growth by CD40-Fc in cultures of striatal MSNs from Cd40-/- mice (p=9.3×10−13) was completely inhibited by Go6983 (p=2.5×10−7).
source: In cultures of striatal MSNs established from E14 Cd40-/- mice, the significant suppression of dendrite growth by CD40-Fc (p=9.3×10−13, Fc treatment compared with CD40-Fc treatment) was completely inhibited by Go6983 (p=2.5×10−7, CD40-Fc treatment compared with CD40-Fc plus Go6983 treatment) and as in hippocampal neuron cultures, Go6983 had no effect on MSN dendrite growth on its own (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of neurite length in cultured MSNs treated with CD40-Fc and Go6983 shown in Figure 5C and D with statistical analysis.

claim: Go6983 had no effect on MSN dendrite growth on its own.
source: In cultures of striatal MSNs established from E14 Cd40-/- mice, the significant suppression of dendrite growth by CD40-Fc (p=9.3×10−13, Fc treatment compared with CD40-Fc treatment) was completely inhibited by Go6983 (p=2.5×10−7, CD40-Fc treatment compared with CD40-Fc plus Go6983 treatment) and as in hippocampal neuron cultures, Go6983 had no effect on MSN dendrite growth on its own (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of neurite length in cultured MSNs treated with Go6983 alone shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: PMA significantly suppressed dendrite growth from MSNs (p=4.5×10−17) to the same extent as CD40-Fc.
source: PMA significantly suppressed dendrite growth from MSNs (p=4.5×10−17) to the same extent as CD40-Fc.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of neurite length in cultured MSNs treated with PMA shown in Figure 5C and D with statistical analysis.

claim: Neither Go6983 nor PMA had any significant effect on the number of MSN primary dendrites.
source: Neither Go6983 nor PMA had any significant effect on the number of MSN primary dendrites (not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text as an experimental result.

claim: PKC activation mediates the effect of CD40-activated CD40L on dendrite growth suppression from developing MSNs.
source: These results suggest that PKC activation mediates the effect of CD40-activated CD40L on dendrite growth suppression from developing MSNs.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental results showing effects of PKC inhibition and activation on dendrite growth in MSNs.

claim: PKC-α, β, γ and ε are abundantly expressed in both the hippocampus and striatum.
source: Using western blotting, we showed abundant expression of PKC-α, β, γ and ε in both the hippocampus and striatum (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: PKC-β and PKC-γ expression can be consistently and efficiently knocked down with specific siRNA in hippocampal and striatal neuron cultures.
source: Because we were able to consistently and efficiently knock down PKC-β and PKC-γ expression with specific siRNA in these cultures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), we focused subsequent experiments on these isoforms.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data showing siRNA knockdown efficiency in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dendrite growth from hippocampal pyramidal neurons transfected with PKC-β siRNA was significantly decreased compared with control siRNA (p=4.9×10−3).
source: Compared with dendrite growth from hippocampal pyramidal neurons transfected with control siRNA, dendrite growth was significantly decreased by PKC-β siRNA (p=4.9×10−3) but not by PKC-γ siRNA (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length in cultured neurons transfected with PKC-β siRNA shown in Figure 6A and B with statistical analysis.

claim: PKC-γ siRNA did not significantly affect dendrite growth from hippocampal pyramidal neurons compared with control siRNA.
source: Compared with dendrite growth from hippocampal pyramidal neurons transfected with control siRNA, dendrite growth was significantly decreased by PKC-β siRNA (p=4.9×10−3) but not by PKC-γ siRNA (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length in cultured neurons transfected with PKC-γ siRNA shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: PKC-γ siRNA, but not PKC-β siRNA, significantly increased dendrite growth from MSNs compared with control siRNA (p=1.6×10−4).
source: Conversely, PKC-γ siRNA but not PKC-β siRNA significantly increased dendrite growth from MSNs compared with control siRNA (p=1.6×10−4) (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of neurite length in cultured MSNs transfected with PKC-γ siRNA shown in Figure 6C and D with statistical analysis.

claim: PKC-β and PKC-γ participate in regulating dendrite growth from developing hippocampal pyramidal neurons and MSNs, respectively.
source: This suggests that PKC-β and PKC-γ participate in regulating dendrite growth from developing hippocampal pyramidal neurons and MSNs, respectively.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the siRNA knockdown experiments showing differential effects of PKC isoforms on different neuron types.

claim: PKC-β siRNA completely prevented CD40-Fc rescue of impaired dendrite growth in CD40-deficient hippocampal pyramidal neurons (p=5.7×10−8).
source: Whereas CD40-Fc rescued the impaired dendrite growth of CD40-deficient hippocampal pyramidal neurons transfected with control siRNA, PKC-β siRNA completely prevented CD40-Fc rescue (p=5.7×10−8) (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dendrite length in cultured Cd40-/- neurons transfected with PKC-β siRNA and treated with CD40-Fc shown in Figure 6A and B with statistical analysis.

claim: PKC-γ siRNA significantly impaired the effect of CD40-Fc in reducing the exuberant dendrite growth of CD40-deficient MSNs (p=7.4×10−4).
source: Whereas CD40-Fc reduced the exuberant dendrite growth of CD40-deficient MSNs transfected with control siRNA, PKC-γ siRNA significantly impaired this effect of CD40-Fc (p=7.4×10−4) (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of neurite length in cultured Cd40-/- MSNs transfected with PKC-γ siRNA and treated with CD40-Fc shown in Figure 6C and D with statistical analysis.

claim: PKC-β and PKC-γ mediate the effects of CD40L reverse signaling in hippocampal pyramidal neurons and MSNs, respectively.
source: Taken together, these results implicate PKC-β and PKC-γ in mediating the effects of CD40L reverse signaling in hippocampal pyramidal neurons and MSNs, respectively.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the siRNA experiments showing that specific PKC isoforms are required for CD40-Fc effects in different neuron types.

claim: Both CD40 and CD40L are expressed in the hippocampus and striatum throughout development and in the adult, with highest levels of both proteins postnatally.
source: Western blotting revealed that both CD40 and CD40L are expressed in the hippocampus and striatum throughout development and in the adult, with highest levels of both proteins postnatally (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD40 immunoreactivity was lost in tissue obtained from Cd40-/- mice, confirming antibody specificity.
source: CD40 immunoreactivity was lost in tissue obtained from Cd40-/- mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), confirming antibody specificity.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data comparing Cd40+/+ and Cd40-/- tissue shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CD40 and CD40L are widely expressed in the hippocampus.
source: Immunohistochemisty revealed that CD40 and CD40L are widely expressed in the hippocampus (Figure 7) and striatum (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 7.

claim: CD40 and CD40L are widely expressed in the striatum.
source: Immunohistochemisty revealed that CD40 and CD40L are widely expressed in the hippocampus (Figure 7) and striatum (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 8.

claim: CD40 and CD40L are expressed throughout the dendrite fields of pyramidal and striatal neurons.
source: Double labelling with anti-MAP2, which labels dendrites, showed that CD40 and CD40L are expressed throughout the dendrite fields of pyramidal and striatal neurons and double labelling with anti-GFAP, which labels astrocytes, showed that CD40 and CD40L are also expressed by these cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by double-labeling immunohistochemistry with MAP2 shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: CD40 and CD40L are expressed by astrocytes.
source: Double labelling with anti-MAP2, which labels dendrites, showed that CD40 and CD40L are expressed throughout the dendrite fields of pyramidal and striatal neurons and double labelling with anti-GFAP, which labels astrocytes, showed that CD40 and CD40L are also expressed by these cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by double-labeling immunohistochemistry with GFAP shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The great majority of pyramidal neurons and MSNs co-express CD40 and CD40L.
source: Double labelling for CD40 and CD40L in dissociated hippocampal and striatal cultures suggest that the great majority of pyramidal neurons and MSNs co-express CD40 and CD40L (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by double-labeling immunocytochemistry in cultured neurons shown in Figure 9.

claim: CD40 is a major novel regulator of dendrite arborisation in the developing brain that exerts prominent disparate effects on major populations of excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: We have discovered that CD40 is a major novel regulator of dendrite arborisation in the developing brain that exerts prominent disparate effects on major populations of excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of all the experimental findings showing opposite effects of CD40 on different neuron types.

claim: CD40 exerts its distinctive effects on dendrite arborisation in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons by a reverse signalling mechanism.
source: These observations together with our demonstration that both hippocampal excitatory and striatal inhibitory neurons display CD40L immunoreactivity, suggests that CD40 exerts its distinctive effects on dendrite arborisation in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons by a reverse signalling mechanism.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental results from CD40L and CD40-Fc treatments combined with immunoreactivity data.

claim: CD40 activates CD40L in both hippocampal pyramidal neurons and striatal MSNs potentially by an autocrine mechanism.
source: Our demonstration that both hippocampal excitatory pyramidal neurons and striatal inhibitory medium spiny neurons co-express CD40L and CD40 raise the possibility that CD40 activates CD40L in both kinds of neurons by an autocrine mechanism.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the co-expression of CD40 and CD40L in the same neurons.

claim: CD40-activated CD40L reverse signaling enhances axon growth from developing sympathetic neurons in vitro and contributes to the establishment of the sympathetic innervation of a specific subset of tissues in vivo.
source: We have previously reported that CD40-activated CD40L reverse signaling enhances axon growth from developing sympathetic neurons in vitro and contributes to the establishment of the sympathetic innervation of a specific subset of tissues in vivo (McWilliams et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (McWilliams et al., 2015).

claim: CD40-activates CD40L in sympathetic neurons by an autocrine mechanism.
source: Because sympathetic neurons co-express CD40 and CD40L and can be cultured at exceptionally low density, it was possible to demonstrate that CD40-activates CD40L in sympathetic neurons by an autocrine mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to previous work on sympathetic neurons.

claim: It has not been possible to exclude the possibility that CD40L is also activated by paracrine mechanism in CNS neurons.
source: Because pyramidal neurons and MSNs have to be grown at much higher density and because these cultures contain a variety of cell types, including glial cells, it has not been possible to exclude the possibility that CD40L is also activated by paracrine mechanism in CNS neurons.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the limitations of the experimental system for determining autocrine vs. paracrine mechanisms.

claim: Microglia express low levels of CD40.
source: Our demonstration that GFAP-positive astrocytes express CD40 and reports that microglia express low levels of CD40 (Carson et al., 1998; Nguyen et al., 1998) raise the possibility that CNS glia may play a role in activating CD40L in neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Carson et al., 1998; Nguyen et al., 1998).

claim: Microglial CD40 may be related primarily to immune function, especially as CD40 is upregulated in these cells by proinflammatory cytokines.
source: However, since CD40L and CD40 play a central role in immune responses (Peters et al., 2009), it is possible that microglial CD40 is related primarily to immune function, especially as CD40 is upregulated in these cells by proinflammatory cytokines (Carson et al., 1998; Nguyen et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the known immune functions of CD40 and citations to previous work.

claim: Several members of the TNFSF regulate axon growth and tissue innervation in developing PNS by either forward or reverse signalling mechanisms.
source: A growing body of evidence has implicated several members of the TNFSF in the regulation of axon growth and tissue innervation in developing PNS by either forward or reverse signalling mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is a summary of previous work in the field.

claim: Individual TNFSF members typically act on restricted populations of PNS neurons and either promote axon growth or inhibit axon growth-promoting effects of neurotrophins.
source: Typically, individual TNFSF members act on restricted populations of PNS neurons and either promote axon growth or inhibit axon growth-promoting effects of neurotrophins (Desbarats et al., 2003; Gavaldà et al., 2009,2013; Kisiswa et al., 2013, 2017; McWilliams et al., 2015; O'Keeffe et al., 2008; Wheeler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is a summary of previous work supported by multiple citations.

claim: CD40-activated CD40L reverse signalling can either promote or inhibit dendritic arborisation in different kinds of neurons.
source: Here we not only demonstrate marked physiologically relevant effects of CD40L reverse signalling on dendrite growth and branching in functionally different kinds of CNS neurons but show that CD40-activated CD40L reverse signalling can either promote or inhibit dendritic arborisation in different kinds of neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of the experimental findings showing opposite effects in different neuron types.

claim: A particular TNFSF member can exert distinctive, neuron-specific effects on CNS dendrite growth.
source: Our work reveals that a particular TNFSF member exerts distinctive, neuron-specific effects on CNS dendrite growth.
evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: CD40 and CD40L are widely expressed in the developing brain neurons.
source: In addition to the hippocampal and striatal neurons studied here, it is clear that CD40 and CD40L are widely expressed in the developing brain neurons (not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on observations not shown in the manuscript.

claim: CD40 may have more widespread effects on the growth of neural processes in the developing brain than those documented in this study.
source: Thus, it is possible that CD40 has more widespread effects on the growth of neural processes in the developing brain than those documented here.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the widespread expression of CD40 and CD40L.

claim: CD40-activated CD40L-mediated reverse signalling may be a physiologically important regulator of pyramidal neuron axon growth in vivo.
source: This raises the possibility that CD40-activated CD40L-mediated reverse signalling may be a physiologically important regulator of pyramidal neuron axon growth in vivo.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the in vitro axon growth data.

claim: The TNFSF member APRIL enhances the axon growth, but not dendrite growth, from cultured hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: We have reported that the TNFSF member APRIL enhances the axon growth, but not dendrite growth, from cultured hippocampal pyramidal neurons (Osório et al., 2014), although the physiological relevance of this observation is unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Osório et al., 2014).

claim: APRIL enhances axon growth from cultured midbrain dopaminergic neurons and the initial nigrostriatal projection is significantly compromised in April-/- embryos.
source: However, we have recently shown that APRIL enhances axon growth from cultured midbrain dopaminergic neurons and that the initial nigrostriatal projection is significantly compromised in April-/- embryos (McWilliams et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to recent work (McWilliams et al., 2017).

claim: CD40 expression is retained in the adult brain, with most of the neurons of the dentate gyrus, hippocampal pyramidal layer and 60% of neurons in cerebral neocortex retaining expression.
source: It has been reported that CD40 expression is retained in the adult brain, with most of the neurons of the dentate gyrus, hippocampal pyramidal layer and 60% of neurons in cerebral neocortex retaining expression (Tan et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Tan et al., 2002).

claim: There is evidence for a neurodegenerative phenotype in aged CD40-deficient mice, with TUNEL-positive cells in the dentate gyrus, hippocampal pyramidal cell layer and neocortex and decreased level of neurofilament isoforms in whole brain lysates.
source: There is also some evidence for a neurodegenerative phenotype in aged CD40-deficient mice, with TUNEL-positive cells in the dentate gyrus, hippocampal pyramidal cell layer and neocortex and decreased level of neurofilament isoforms in whole brain lysates (Tan et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Tan et al., 2002).

claim: The marked reduction in the size and complexity of pyramidal neuron dendritic arbors in the postnatal and adult brain may contribute to late degenerative changes by impairing trophic maintenance of the degenerating neurons.
source: Although the reason for these late degenerative changes is unclear, it is possible that the marked reduction in the size and complexity of pyramidal neuron dendritic arbors that we have documented in the postnatal and adult brain may contribute by impairing trophic maintenance of the degenerating neurons.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the potential consequences of the observed dendrite phenotype.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of PKC completely prevented the rescue of the distinctive dendrite phenotypes of CD40-deficient hippocampal and striatal neurons by soluble CD40-Fc.
source: Our demonstration that pharmacological inhibition of PKC completely prevented the rescue of the distinctive dendrite phenotypes of CD40-deficient hippocampal and striatal neurons by soluble CD40-Fc and that pharmacological activation of PKC was as effective as CD40-Fc in rescuing these phenotypes suggests that PKC activation is an essential step in the effect of CD40-activated CD40L reverse signalling on dendrite growth in both kinds of neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the PKC inhibition experiments with Go6983.

claim: Pharmacological activation of PKC was as effective as CD40-Fc in rescuing the dendrite phenotypes of CD40-deficient hippocampal and striatal neurons.
source: Our demonstration that pharmacological inhibition of PKC completely prevented the rescue of the distinctive dendrite phenotypes of CD40-deficient hippocampal and striatal neurons by soluble CD40-Fc and that pharmacological activation of PKC was as effective as CD40-Fc in rescuing these phenotypes suggests that PKC activation is an essential step in the effect of CD40-activated CD40L reverse signalling on dendrite growth in both kinds of neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the PKC activation experiments with PMA.

claim: PKC activation is an essential step in the effect of CD40-activated CD40L reverse signalling on dendrite growth in both hippocampal pyramidal neurons and striatal MSNs.
source: Our demonstration that pharmacological inhibition of PKC completely prevented the rescue of the distinctive dendrite phenotypes of CD40-deficient hippocampal and striatal neurons by soluble CD40-Fc and that pharmacological activation of PKC was as effective as CD40-Fc in rescuing these phenotypes suggests that PKC activation is an essential step in the effect of CD40-activated CD40L reverse signalling on dendrite growth in both kinds of neurons.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the PKC inhibition and activation experiments.

claim: PKC activation mediates both the growth-promoting and growth-inhibitory effects of reverse signaling in different kinds of neurons.
source: This finding extends the importance of PKC in mediating the axon growth response of developing sympathetic neurons to TNFR1-activated TNF reverse signaling (Kisiswa et al., 2017) to another example of TNFSF reverse signaling affecting neural process growth. Moreover, it shows that PKC activation mediates both the growth-promoting and growth-inhibitory effects of reverse signaling in different kinds of neurons.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the PKC experiments showing opposite effects in different neuron types.

claim: PKC inhibition prevents enhanced neurite growth from cultured embryonic hippocampal neurons by neuregulin-1.
source: PKC inhibition also prevents enhanced neurite growth from cultured embryonic hippocampal neurons by neuregulin-1 (Gerecke et al., 2004), whereas PKC activation increases dendrite growth and branching from these neurons by modulating neurotrophin synthesis (Lim and Alkon, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Gerecke et al., 2004).

claim: PKC activation increases dendrite growth and branching from hippocampal neurons by modulating neurotrophin synthesis.
source: PKC inhibition also prevents enhanced neurite growth from cultured embryonic hippocampal neurons by neuregulin-1 (Gerecke et al., 2004), whereas PKC activation increases dendrite growth and branching from these neurons by modulating neurotrophin synthesis (Lim and Alkon, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Lim and Alkon, 2012).

claim: CD40L reverse signalling extends from modulating the growth of a subset of sympathetic axons in the PNS to that of a major, physiologically relevant regulator of dendrite growth and elaboration in the developing CNS.
source: Our current study extends the role of CD40L reverse signalling from modulating the growth of a subset of sympathetic axons in the PNS to that of a major, physiologically relevant regulator of dendrite growth and elaboration in the developing CNS, having distinctive and opposite effects on excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of the study's findings in the context of previous work.

claim: Dendrite size and morphology are key determinants of the functional properties of neurons and neural circuits.
source: Dendrite size and morphology are key determinants of the functional properties of neurons and neural circuits.
evidence: The claim is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: Many neurodevelopmental and acquired disorders of neural function are due primarily to structural abnormalities of dendrites and their connections.
source: The regulation of dendrite growth and elaboration during development has a major bearing on the functional properties of neurons and neural circuits, and many neurodevelopmental and acquired disorders of neural function are due primarily to structural abnormalities of dendrites and their connections (Penzes et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Penzes et al., 2011).

claim: A wide variety of extrinsic signals orchestrate the growth and remodeling of dendrites during development and maturation, including delta-notch, Eph-Ephrins, cell adhesion molecules, neurotrophins, semaphorins and slits.
source: In addition to intrinsic developmental programmes and the pattern of electrical activity, a wide variety of extrinsic signals orchestrate the growth and remodeling of dendrites during development and maturation, including delta-notch, Eph-Ephrins, cell adhesion molecules, neurotrophins, semaphorins and slits (Metzger, 2010; Valnegri et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Metzger, 2010; Valnegri et al., 2015).

claim: The tumor necrosis factor superfamily (TNFSF) is one of the latest groups of proteins recognized to modulate growth of neural processes during development.
source: One of the latest groups of proteins recognized to modulate growth of neural processes during development is the tumor necrosis factor superfamily (TNFSF), the 19 members of which are best understood for their many roles in the immune system (Hehlgans and Pfeffer, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Hehlgans and Pfeffer, 2005).

claim: TNFSF members are active both as membrane-integrated ligands and as soluble ligands following cleavage from the cell membrane.
source: They are active both as membrane-integrated ligands and as soluble ligands following cleavage from the cell membrane, and bind to one or more members of the TNF receptor superfamily (TNFRSF).
evidence: The claim is a statement of established knowledge about TNFSF members.

claim: Several TNFRSF members can function as ligands for membrane-integrated TNFSF binding partners and initiate reverse signalling.
source: In addition, several TNFRSF members can also function as ligands for membrane-integrated TNFSF binding partners and initiate reverse signalling (Sun and Fink, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Sun and Fink, 2007).

claim: CD40 and its ligand CD40L play key roles in immune responses and in the pathogenesis of autoimmune disease.
source: CD40 and its ligand CD40L play key roles in immune responses and in the pathogenesis of autoimmune disease (Peters et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Peters et al., 2009).

claim: CD40 and CD40L have been implicated in regulating sympathetic axon growth and are required for establishing the innervation of particular tissues in the developing PNS.
source: CD40 and CD40L have also recently been implicated in regulating sympathetic axon growth and are required for establishing the innervation of particular tissues in the developing PNS (McWilliams et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (McWilliams et al., 2015).

claim: Hippocampal pyramidal neurons are one of the best-characterized models for studying the differentiation and growth of axons and dendrites during development.
source: Hippocampal pyramidal neurons are one of the best-characterized models for studying the differentiation and growth of axons and dendrites during development (Kaech and Banker, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Kaech and Banker, 2006).

claim: MSNs comprise the majority of neurons in the striatum, have extensive dendritic arbors, project to the surrounding nuclei of the basal ganglia.
source: MSNs comprise the majority of neurons in the striatum, have extensive dendritic arbors, project to the surrounding nuclei of the basal ganglia and their degeneration is the pathognomonic feature of Huntington's disease (Reiner et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Reiner et al., 1988).

claim: Degeneration of MSNs is the pathognomonic feature of Huntington's disease.
source: MSNs comprise the majority of neurons in the striatum, have extensive dendritic arbors, project to the surrounding nuclei of the basal ganglia and their degeneration is the pathognomonic feature of Huntington's disease (Reiner et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Reiner et al., 1988).

claim: Cd40 null mutant mice were back-crossed for at least 10 generations into a CD1 background before undertaking experimental work.
source: Cd40 null mutant mice in a C57BL6/J background were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, Maine, USA). These mice were back-crossed for at least 10 generations into a CD1 background before undertaking any of the current experimental work.
evidence: The claim is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Hippocampal neuron cultures were established from E18 mice and by 9 days in vitro, MAP-2-positive dendrites can be unambiguously identified and quantified.
source: Hippocampal pyramidal neuron cultures were established from E18 mice. By 9 days in vitro, MAP-2-positive dendrites can be unambiguously identified and quantified (Kaech and Banker, 2006; Osório et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is a description of the experimental methods supported by citations.

claim: MSN cultures were established from E14 striatal primordia.
source: MSN cultures were established from E14 striatal primordia.
evidence: The claim is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: DARPP-32 is expressed by more than 95% of MSNs.
source: For this reason, we positively identified MSNs using an antibody to dopamine and cyclic AMP-regulated protein (DARPP-32), which is expressed by more than 95% of MSNs (Ouimet et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Ouimet et al., 1998).
